analysis.one_liner: Bans domestic manufacture, sale, and possession of cheap, low-quality 'junk guns' that cannot legally be imported.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban domestic 'junk gun' manufacture died in a House Judiciary subcommittee in 1996 without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1968, federal law has barred importing cheap handguns that fail a 'sporting purposes' test — but the same low-quality guns, often called Saturday night specials, could still be made and sold by American manufacturers. This bill would make it a federal crime to manufacture, transfer, or possess such a gun in interstate commerce, while exempting guns people already owned, law enforcement, and permanently inoperative firearms. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee's Crime subcommittee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People in high-crime neighborhoods, where cheap, poorly made handguns are disproportionately used in crimes and traced by police most often, plus law enforcement officers who face these weapons. Honest gun manufacturers who already meet quality and safety standards would also face less low-price competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of high-crime neighborhoods and police

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to manufacture, transfer, or possess a 'junk gun' — defined as any handgun that does not meet the standards already used to bar such guns from importation — when shipped in interstate or foreign commerce.

The bill's findings state that the three firearms most commonly traced to crimes in 1995 were junk guns, and that these weapons are used disproportionately in crimes, posing a threat to the public and to police.
It closes a loophole where the same gun banned from import could be manufactured domestically, 'apply[ing] equal standards to certain foreign made and domestically produced handguns.'
Grandfathers guns lawfully possessed before enactment and exempts law enforcement and authorized testing, so the ban targets the new market for these weapons rather than existing owners.

analysis.who_pays: Domestic manufacturers of inexpensive, low-quality handguns, which would lose their product line, and federally licensed dealers who sell them. Buyers of cheap handguns would lose access to the lowest-priced new weapons.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cheap handgun manufacturers and their dealers

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches possession, not just manufacture and sale, which is broader than an import-style rule and could sweep in otherwise lawful transfers of inexpensive handguns in interstate commerce.

The 'junk gun' definition is tied to the existing import standard, a regulatory test that critics of gun control argue is vague and could sweep in inexpensive but serviceable handguns, restricting access to the cheapest means of self-defense for low-income buyers.

A domestic-only manufacturing ban leaves the underlying demand for cheap crime guns in place; a good-faith objection is that it displaces supply rather than reducing violence, at real cost to a lawful domestic industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but one-sided in design: the bill simply extends to domestic manufacturers the same quality standard imported guns must already meet, and it grandfathers existing owners, so the cost falls mainly on one slice of the firearms industry rather than on gun owners broadly. The strongest objection is that possession coverage and the regulatory definition could reach farther than intended, and that suppressing supply of a product people demand rarely eliminates the market. On balance the bill is modestly designed for its goal, but it was never tested in debate or amendment.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its Crime subcommittee two weeks later, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jack Reed introduced the Junk Gun Violence Protection Act on June 13, 1996, with 18 original cosponsors including Reps. Schumer, Pelosi, and Waxman.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction.
On June 26, 1996, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, where it remained with no further action through the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic makers of inexpensive handguns, who kept a market the import ban had closed to foreign competitors, and no one else in particular — the bill simply expired without a fight.

for.name: Rep. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on June 13-14, 1996.

for.name: Rep. Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

for.name: 20 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship at introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 13, 1996, and referred it to the Subcommittee on Crime on June 26; no hearing, markup, or vote followed before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman in the 104th Congress, controlled the committee's agenda; the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was mostly Democratic (17 of 20 cosponsors) but included 3 Republicans, and no recorded vote ever tested the split; the bill died quietly at the subcommittee stage rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Domestic manufacturers of inexpensive handguns ('Saturday night special' makers)
industries.note: The bill would prohibit manufacture, transfer, and possession of guns these firms make, closing a market created when the 1968 import ban applied only to foreign guns. Their cheapest products are the ones most often traced to crimes, so their interest in blocking the bill ran against the public-safety aim.

industries.industry: Federally licensed firearms dealers and importers
industries.note: Dealers would lose sales of the lowest-priced handguns, but the grandfathring of existing stock limited losses. Importers already face the same quality standard, so the bill leveled rather than added restrictions for them.
